source.text: וַיֹּ֣סֶף אִ֭יּוֹב שְׂאֵ֥ת מְשָׁל֗וֹ וַיֹּאמַֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And added Job to-take-up his discourse and said:

en.L: And Job again took up his discourse and said:
en.B: Job took up his discourse again and said:
en.R: Then Job spoke again:

decisions.choice: Job went on: he speaks again with no friend answering in between
alternatives: Job answered (as at the start of the earlier speeches)
decisions.reason: Every speech so far has opened with "answered and said" (3:2; 4:1; 6:1 ... 26:1). Here the words are different: Job "added" to his speech, that is, he continued. Bildad's last speech (chapter 25) was short, and Zophar, who spoke in chapters 11 and 20, does not speak a third time. The same words open 29:1.

decisions.choice: discourse: a weighty speech, a poem with a lesson
decisions.reason: Mashal is a proverb or a solemn poem that teaches, like Balaam's oracles (Numbers 23:7) or a wisdom psalm (Psalm 49:5; 78:2). It marks what follows as a considered address, not only a reply.

decisions.choice: took up his discourse again (B), spoke again (R)
alternatives: continued to take up his discourse
decisions.reason: Hebrew says Job "added to take up": he did it again. Balanced says "again"; Readable says simply that he spoke again, following the book-wide pattern for speech openings.

source.text: חַי־אֵ֭ל הֵסִ֣יר מִשְׁפָּטִ֑י וְ֝שַׁדַּ֗י הֵמַ֥ר נַפְשִֽׁי׃

records.literal_gloss: [By the] life [of] God [who] has taken away my right, and [the] Almighty [who] has made bitter my soul,

en.L: [As] God lives, [who] has taken away my right, \q and the Almighty, [who] has made my soul bitter,
en.B: As God lives, who has denied me justice, \q and the Almighty, who has made my life bitter,
en.R: I swear by the living God, who has refused me justice, \q by God All-Powerful, who has made my life bitter:

decisions.choice: as God lives: a solemn oath
decisions.reason: "As God lives" opens an oath (Ruth 3:13; 1 Samuel 14:39; 20:3). What Job swears follows in 27:3-4. He swears by the life of the very God he says has wronged him: he still holds to God while accusing him.

decisions.choice: my right: the justice I am owed, a fair verdict
decisions.reason: Mishpat is the verdict or the right a person is owed in court. Job says God has kept him from getting justice (19:7). Elihu later quotes these words against him (34:5).

decisions.choice: the Almighty has made my soul bitter
decisions.reason: Naomi said almost the same of herself: "the Almighty has made me very bitter" (Ruth 1:20). Soul (nefesh) is the whole person, so the bitterness is in Job's whole life. On the Almighty (Shaddai) see 5:17.

decisions.choice: I swear by the living God
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that Job is taking an oath (m1), since "as God lives" is no longer a familiar way to swear.

source.text: כִּֽי־כָל־ע֣וֹד נִשְׁמָתִ֣י בִ֑י וְר֖וּחַ אֱל֣וֹהַּ בְּאַפִּֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: for all still my breath [is] in me, and [the] breath of God [is] in my nose,

en.L: for as long as my breath [is] in me, \q and the breath of God [is] in my nostrils,
en.B: as long as I still have breath in me \q and the breath of God is in my nostrils,
en.R: as long as I am alive \q and God's breath of life is in me,

decisions.choice: as long as: the whole time that
alternatives: for my breath is still wholly in me
decisions.reason: "All still" means "all the while". The words set how long the oath holds: as long as Job lives. The opening ki here belongs to the oath and does not give a reason.

decisions.choice: the breath of God in my nostrils: life as God's gift
decisions.reason: God breathed the breath of life into the first man's nostrils (Genesis 2:7). Job says his life is breath from God, as Elihu also says (33:4) and as 34:14-15 says God could take back.

decisions.choice: breath (ruach), not spirit
decisions.reason: Ruach is paired here with neshamah, "breath", and placed in the nostrils, so it means the breath of life.

decisions.choice: as long as I am alive / God's breath of life
alternatives: as long as my breath is in me
decisions.reason: Readable says what having breath means, being alive, and adds "of life" to show that God's breath is what keeps Job alive (m2).

source.text: אִם־תְּדַבֵּ֣רְנָה שְׂפָתַ֣י עַוְלָ֑ה וּ֝לְשׁוֹנִ֗י אִם־יֶהְגֶּ֥ה רְמִיָּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: If will speak my lips injustice, and my tongue if will utter deceit.

en.L: my lips will not speak injustice, \q and my tongue will not utter deceit.
en.B: my lips will not speak what is wrong, \q and my tongue will not utter lies.
en.R: I will never say anything wrong, \q and I will never tell a lie.

decisions.choice: "if" in an oath: surely not
decisions.reason: In a Hebrew oath, "if" with the curse left unsaid ("may God punish me if ...") means "certainly not" (Genesis 14:23; 1 Samuel 3:17; Psalm 95:11). Job swears that he will not speak falsely.

decisions.choice: injustice, deceit: here, a false confession of guilt
decisions.reason: The next verses show what lie Job refuses to tell: to agree with the friends that he deserves his suffering (27:5-6) would be untrue.

decisions.choice: lips ... tongue become plain speech at Readable
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps lips and tongue; Readable says "I will never say", since the body parts stand for Job's speaking.

source.text: חָלִ֣ילָה לִּי֮ אִם־אַצְדִּ֪יק אֶ֫תְכֶ֥ם עַד־אֶגְוָ֑ע לֹא־אָסִ֖יר תֻּמָּתִ֣י מִמֶּֽנִּי׃

records.literal_gloss: Far be it to me if I declare right you; until I expire not I will put away my integrity from me.

en.L: Far be it from me that I should declare you right; \q until I die \q I will not put away my integrity from me.
en.B: Far be it from me to say that you are right; \q until I die \q I will not give up my integrity.
en.R: I will never say that you are right. \q Until the day I die, I will not give up my integrity.

decisions.choice: far be it from me: a strong refusal
decisions.reason: The word comes from a root meaning "profane": it would be an unholy thing for me (Genesis 18:25; 1 Samuel 24:7).

decisions.choice: declare you right: grant that you are in the right in this dispute
decisions.reason: This form of the verb is a court word: to declare someone in the right (Deuteronomy 25:1). "You" is plural, the friends. Job will not concede their case against him.

decisions.choice: integrity: the wholeness of a blameless life
decisions.reason: Tummah comes from the same root as "blameless" (1:1). God said Job still held to his integrity (2:3), and his wife asked why he did (2:9). Job now swears to keep it.

source.text: בְּצִדְקָתִ֣י הֶ֭חֱזַקְתִּי וְלֹ֣א אַרְפֶּ֑הָ לֹֽא־יֶחֱרַ֥ף לְ֝בָבִ֗י מִיָּמָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: On my righteousness I have held fast and not I will let it go; not reproaches my heart from my days.

en.L: I have held fast to my righteousness and will not let it go; \q my heart does not reproach [me] \q for any of my days.
en.B: I hold on to my righteousness and will not let it go; \q my conscience does not blame me \q for any day of my life.
en.R: I will hold on to my claim that I have done right, and I will not let it go. \q My conscience does not accuse me for any day of my life.

decisions.choice: my righteousness: my being in the right in this case
decisions.reason: Job does not claim never to have sinned (7:21; 13:26). He claims that he has done nothing to deserve what has happened and that his cause is just.

decisions.choice: my heart does not reproach me: my conscience is clear
decisions.reason: The heart can strike or rebuke a person, as David's heart struck him (1 Samuel 24:6; 25:31). It is what we call the conscience.

decisions.choice: for any of my days: about any day of my life
alternatives: as long as I live (my heart will not reproach me)
decisions.reason: "From my days" can mean that no day of Job's past gives his conscience cause to accuse him, or that it will not accuse him for the rest of his life. The first fits the claim of the first line.

decisions.choice: conscience
decisions.reason: In English, the heart does not reproach anyone; the conscience does (m2).

source.text: יְהִ֣י כְ֭רָשָׁע אֹ֣יְבִ֑י וּמִתְקוֹמְמִ֥י כְעַוָּֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: May be like [the] wicked my enemy, and [the one] raising himself against me like [the] unjust.

en.L: May my enemy be like the wicked, \q and the one who rises against me like the unjust.
en.B: Let my enemy be like the wicked, \q and my opponent like the unrighteous.
en.R: May my enemy end up like the wicked. \q May the one who attacks me be treated like someone who does evil.

decisions.choice: a wish: may my enemy share the fate of the wicked
alternatives: my enemy is like the wicked (a statement)
decisions.reason: The verb is a wish. Job turns the friends' descriptions of the end of the wicked (chapters 8, 15, 18, 20) on whoever opposes him.

decisions.choice: my enemy, the one who rises against me: whoever accuses him
decisions.reason: In a court the one who "rises up" against someone is the accuser (Deuteronomy 19:16; Psalm 27:12). Job does not name him; the friends, who have charged him with great wickedness (22:5), are near at hand.

decisions.choice: end up like ... be treated like
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that Job wishes his enemy the fate of the wicked, not their character (m1).

source.text: כִּ֤י מַה־תִּקְוַ֣ת חָ֭נֵף כִּ֣י יִבְצָ֑ע כִּ֤י יֵ֖שֶׁל אֱל֣וֹהַּ נַפְשֽׁוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: For what [is the] hope of [the] godless when he cuts off, when draws out God his life?

en.L: For what [is the] hope of the godless when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} cuts [him] off, \q when God takes away his life?
en.B: For what hope does the godless have when God cuts him off, \q when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} takes away his life?
en.R: What hope does a godless person have \q when God ends his life and takes it away?

decisions.choice: cuts off: God ends the life of the godless
alternatives: however much he gains (the same verb means to make a profit)
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to cut off, as a weaver cuts the thread from the loom (Isaiah 38:12), or to gain, often unjustly. The second line, "when God takes away his life", favors cutting off, with God as the subject of both.

decisions.choice: the hope of the godless
decisions.reason: Bildad said that "the hope of the godless will perish" (8:13). Job agrees: a godless person has nothing to hope for at death. He is not such a person (13:16).

decisions.choice: draws out, takes away
decisions.reason: The verb is rare; it means to pull out or draw off, here the life (nefesh) drawn out of a person.

decisions.choice: God named in the first line
alternatives: he cuts off ... when God takes
decisions.reason: Hebrew names God only in the second line. Balanced and Readable name him at once, so that the reader knows who cuts the godless off.

decisions.choice: his life (the godless pictured as a man)
decisions.reason: Job's picture of the wicked here and in 27:13-23 is of a man with sons and widows, so the pronouns stay "he" and "his".

source.text: הַֽ֭צַעֲקָתוֹ יִשְׁמַ֥ע׀אֵ֑ל כִּֽי־תָב֖וֹא עָלָ֣יו צָרָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: His cry will hear God when comes upon him distress?

en.L: Will God hear his cry \q when distress comes upon him?
en.B: Will God hear his cry \q when trouble comes upon him?
en.R: When trouble comes on him, \q will God listen when he cries for help?

decisions.choice: a question expecting "no"
decisions.reason: The question mark at the head of the verse expects the answer no: God will not answer the godless when disaster comes (Proverbs 1:28; Micah 3:4).

decisions.choice: cry: a cry for help in distress
decisions.reason: Tse'aqah is the cry of the oppressed (Exodus 3:7). Job himself cries out and gets no answer (19:7; 30:20), but he does not count himself among the godless.

decisions.choice: the time clause first
alternatives: Will God hear his cry when trouble comes?
decisions.reason: Readable puts the time first, as plain English tends to, without change of sense.

source.text: אִם־עַל־שַׁדַּ֥י יִתְעַנָּ֑ג יִקְרָ֖א אֱל֣וֹהַּ בְּכָל־עֵֽת׃

records.literal_gloss: Or on [the] Almighty will he take delight? Will he call [on] God at every time?

en.L: Or will he take delight in the Almighty? \q Will he call on God at all times?
en.B: Will he find delight in the Almighty? \q Will he call on God at all times?
en.R: Will he find his delight in God All-Powerful? \q Will he pray to God all the time?

decisions.choice: delight in the Almighty
decisions.reason: Eliphaz promised Job that if he returned to God he would "delight in the Almighty" (22:26, the same words). Job says that such delight, and steady prayer, belong to the person who truly holds to God, not to the godless.

decisions.choice: call on God at all times: keep praying in every situation
decisions.reason: The godless person may cry out in distress (27:9), but does not keep calling on God. Job, for all his complaint, has never stopped speaking to God.

decisions.choice: pray to
decisions.reason: "Call on God" means to pray to him; Readable says so.

source.text: אוֹרֶ֣ה אֶתְכֶ֣ם בְּיַד־אֵ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר עִם־שַׁ֝דַּ֗י לֹ֣א אֲכַחֵֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: I will teach you about [the] hand of God; what [is] with [the] Almighty not I will hide.

en.L: I will teach you about the hand of God; \q what [is] with the Almighty \q I will not hide.
en.B: I will teach you about the power of God; \q what the Almighty has in mind \q I will not hide.
en.R: I will teach you about the power of God. \q I will not hide from you how God All-Powerful works.

decisions.choice: the hand of God: God's power and what he does with it
decisions.reason: The hand stands for power and action (12:9-10; 19:21). Job will speak of what God does.

decisions.choice: what is with the Almighty: God's ways and purposes
decisions.reason: What is "with" someone is what they hold in mind or plan (10:13; 23:14). Job says he knows these as well as the friends.

decisions.choice: you (plural): Job speaks to all three friends
decisions.reason: The pronoun is plural, as in 27:5 and 27:12.

decisions.choice: power ... has in mind (B), how God works (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the pictures mean (m1, m2).

source.text: הֵן־אַתֶּ֣ם כֻּלְּכֶ֣ם חֲזִיתֶ֑ם וְלָמָּה־זֶּ֝֗ה הֶ֣בֶל תֶּהְבָּֽלוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Look, you, all of you have seen; and why [is] this [that] vanity you become vain?

en.L: Look, you yourselves, all of you, have seen [it]; \q so why then do you become empty [with] emptiness?
en.B: Look, all of you have seen it for yourselves; \q why then do you talk such empty nonsense?
en.R: You have all seen this for yourselves. \q So why do you keep saying things that mean nothing?

decisions.choice: become vain with vanity: talk emptily, speak nonsense
decisions.reason: Hevel is breath or vapor, something without substance (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Here noun and verb from the same root are put together: you are puffing out empty breath. Job used the word of their comfort in 21:34.

decisions.choice: you have seen: the friends know how things are
decisions.reason: Job says the friends have seen for themselves how God deals with the wicked, so their charges against him have no ground.

decisions.choice: why then: "this" adds force to the question
decisions.reason: Hebrew adds "this" to a question for emphasis: why ever, why then.

decisions.choice: talk such empty nonsense (B), saying things that mean nothing (R)
decisions.reason: English cannot repeat one word as noun and verb here. Balanced uses "empty" and "nonsense" to keep the force of the wordplay (m1).

source.text: זֶ֤ה׀חֵֽלֶק־אָדָ֖ם רָשָׁ֥ע׀עִם־אֵ֑ל וְֽנַחֲלַ֥ת עָ֝רִיצִ֗ים מִשַּׁדַּ֥י יִקָּֽחוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: This [is the] portion of a person wicked with God, and [the] inheritance of ruthless [ones] [which] from [the] Almighty they will receive.

en.L: This [is the] portion of a wicked {{gender:person|man}} with God, \q and the inheritance of the ruthless, \q [which] they receive from the Almighty.
en.B: This is the portion a wicked {{gender:person|man}} has from God, \q the inheritance the ruthless receive from the Almighty:
en.R: This is what God has in store for a wicked person. \q This is what cruel people receive from God All-Powerful:

decisions.choice: Job takes up Zophar's words
decisions.reason: Zophar ended his second speech with nearly the same line: "This is the portion of a wicked person from God, the inheritance appointed him by God" (20:29). Job repeats it and goes on to describe the end of the wicked in the friends' own manner.

decisions.choice: the words are Job's: he grants that God will punish the wicked and turns the warning on his accusers
alternatives: Job is quoting the friends' view in order to mock it
27:13-23 belong to a third speech of Zophar that is missing from the text as we have it
decisions.reason: In 21:7-34 Job said that the wicked often live long and prosper; here he describes their ruin. The text gives these words to Job (27:1), and he has just warned that his enemy should fare like the wicked (27:7). Because Zophar has no third speech and Bildad's is very short (chapter 25), some readers think the speeches of this cycle have been disordered. The Hebrew text as it stands is translated here.

decisions.choice: the ruthless: violent oppressors, tyrants
decisions.reason: 'Aritsim are people who use terror and force (6:23; 15:20, where Eliphaz uses the same pair as here).

decisions.choice: a wicked person (gender setting, with "man" as the alternative), then "he" in 27:14-23
decisions.reason: Adam here means a human being, so the noun takes the gender setting. The picture that follows is of a householder with sons and widows (27:14-15), so the pronouns in 27:14-23 stay "he" and "his" at every level.

source.text: אִם־יִרְבּ֣וּ בָנָ֣יו לְמוֹ־חָ֑רֶב וְ֝צֶאֱצָאָ֗יו לֹ֣א יִשְׂבְּעוּ־לָֽחֶם׃

records.literal_gloss: If increase his sons, for [the] sword [they are]; and his offspring not will be satisfied [with] bread.

en.L: If his sons become many, [it is] for the sword, \q and his offspring will not be satisfied [with] bread.
en.B: If his children are many, they are destined for the sword, \q and his descendants will never have enough to eat.
en.R: He may have many children, but they will be killed in war. \q His descendants will go hungry.

decisions.choice: if ... for the sword: the more children, the more for the sword
decisions.reason: "If" here means "even if" or "however many": a large family, a sign of blessing, will only give more victims to violence (compare 5:4; 18:19; 20:10).

decisions.choice: his sons: his children, his line
decisions.reason: Banim is "sons", and the next line speaks more widely of his offspring: his whole family line will suffer.

decisions.choice: not satisfied with bread: they will go hungry
decisions.reason: Bread stands for food in general.

decisions.choice: killed in war
decisions.reason: The sword stands for violent death, in war or by the hand of enemies; Readable says what it means.

source.text: שְׂ֭רִידָיו בַּמָּ֣וֶת יִקָּבֵ֑רוּ וְ֝אַלְמְנֹתָ֗יו לֹ֣א תִבְכֶּֽינָה׃

records.literal_gloss: His survivors by death will be buried, and his widows not will weep.

en.L: His survivors will be buried by death, \q and his widows will not weep.
en.B: Those who survive him will be buried by the plague, \q and his widows will not mourn.
en.R: Those of his family who are left will die of disease and be buried, \q and his widows will not even cry for them.

decisions.choice: death: deadly disease, plague
decisions.reason: Death here, as in Jeremiah 15:2 and 18:21, is a deadly disease that sweeps people away. Those who escape the sword (27:14) fall to plague.

decisions.choice: his widows do not weep: there are no proper mourning rites
decisions.reason: To be buried without the mourning of one's family was a mark of disgrace and disaster; Psalm 78:64 uses the same words. The plural "widows" fits a wealthy man with more than one wife.

decisions.choice: the plague
decisions.reason: "Buried by death" makes little sense in English; Balanced names the deadly disease meant (m1).

source.text: אִם־יִצְבֹּ֣ר כֶּעָפָ֣ר כָּ֑סֶף וְ֝כַחֹ֗מֶר יָכִ֥ין מַלְבּֽוּשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: If he heaps up like dust silver, and like clay he prepares clothing,

en.L: If he heaps up silver like dust, \q and lays up clothing like clay,
en.B: Though he piles up silver like dust \q and stores up clothes like heaps of clay,
en.R: He may pile up silver like dust \q and stack up clothes like piles of clay.

decisions.choice: like dust, like clay: in huge amounts
decisions.reason: Dust and clay are what there is most of. Zechariah 9:3 uses the same picture: Tyre "heaped up silver like dust, and gold like the mud of the streets".

decisions.choice: clothing: a form of wealth
decisions.reason: Fine garments were stored and given as wealth (Genesis 45:22; Joshua 7:21; 2 Kings 5:5, 22).

decisions.choice: heaps of clay (B), piles of clay (R)
decisions.reason: "Heaps" and "piles" make the point of the comparison, the amount, clear in English.

source.text: יָ֭כִין וְצַדִּ֣יק יִלְבָּ֑שׁ וְ֝כֶ֗סֶף נָקִ֥י יַחֲלֹֽק׃

records.literal_gloss: he will prepare [it], but [the] righteous will wear [it], and [the] silver [the] innocent will divide.

en.L: he may lay [it] up, but the righteous will wear [it], \q and the innocent will divide the silver.
en.B: he may store them up, but the righteous will wear them, \q and the innocent will divide up the silver.
en.R: But good people will wear his clothes, \q and innocent people will share his silver.

decisions.choice: the wealth of the wicked passes to the righteous
decisions.reason: A common teaching of the wise: "the sinner's wealth is stored up for the righteous" (Proverbs 13:22; 28:8; Ecclesiastes 2:26).

decisions.choice: he may store it up: the verb picks up the end of 27:16
decisions.reason: The verb that ends 27:16 opens 27:17. The wicked man prepares, but others enjoy what he prepared.

decisions.choice: good people ... innocent people
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words; the Hebrew terms are singular but stand for the whole class.

source.text: בָּנָ֣ה כָעָ֣שׁ בֵּית֑וֹ וּ֝כְסֻכָּ֗ה עָשָׂ֥ה נֹצֵֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: He has built like the moth his house, and like a booth [that] has made a watchman.

en.L: He has built his house like the moth, \q and like a hut [that] a watchman has made.
en.B: The house he builds is like a moth's cocoon, \q like a shelter put up by a watchman.
en.R: The house he builds is as weak as a moth's cocoon, \q as flimsy as a hut that a field guard puts up.

decisions.choice: like the moth: as frail as the case a moth builds
decisions.reason: A moth's "house" is its cocoon, a flimsy thing; the moth is a picture of frailty in 4:19 and 13:28. Some ancient translations speak of a spider here, as in Bildad's picture of the godless person's trust as a spider's house (8:14).

decisions.choice: a watchman's hut: a temporary shelter in a field or vineyard
decisions.reason: At harvest a guard watched the crop from a booth of branches, put up for a season and then left to fall (Isaiah 1:8; 24:20).

decisions.choice: cocoon
decisions.reason: "Built his house like the moth" could be read as the moth eating the house. Balanced and Readable name the moth's house, the cocoon (m1).

source.text: עָשִׁ֣יר יִ֭שְׁכַּב וְלֹ֣א יֵאָסֵ֑ף עֵינָ֖יו פָּקַ֣ח וְאֵינֶֽנּוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Rich he lies down, and not he will be gathered; his eyes he opens, and he [is] not.

en.L: Rich he lies down, but he will not be gathered; \q he opens his eyes, and he is no more.
en.B: He lies down rich, but he will not be gathered to his ancestors; \q he opens his eyes, and he is gone.
en.R: He goes to bed rich, but he will not be buried with his family. \q In a moment he is gone.

decisions.choice: not gathered: not laid to rest with his ancestors
alternatives: he will not do so again (the reading of some ancient translations)
his wealth will not be gathered in
decisions.reason: "To be gathered" is said of dying and being buried with one's people (Numbers 20:26; Genesis 25:8), and "not gathered" of the dead left unburied (Jeremiah 8:2; Ezekiel 29:5). The ancient Greek translation reads "he will not add", that is, he will lie down rich no more, from a word with almost the same letters. The Hebrew text is translated here.

decisions.choice: he opens his eyes, and he is gone: sudden ruin
alternatives: he opens his eyes and his wealth is gone
decisions.reason: The picture is of a man who lies down at night rich and secure, and is swept away before he knows it (27:20). "He is not" is said of someone who has vanished or died (7:8, 21).

decisions.choice: to his ancestors (B), buried with his family (R)
decisions.reason: "Gathered" alone would mean little to an English reader; Balanced and Readable say what the idiom means (m1).

decisions.choice: In a moment
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the picture, how suddenly the end comes (m2).

source.text: תַּשִּׂיגֵ֣הוּ כַ֭מַּיִם בַּלָּה֑וֹת לַ֝֗יְלָה גְּנָבַ֥תּוּ סוּפָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Overtake him like waters terrors; [by] night steals him away a storm.

en.L: Terrors overtake him like waters; \q [by] night a storm steals him away.
en.B: Terrors overtake him like a flood; \q in the night a storm carries him off.
en.R: Terrors sweep over him like a flood. \q A storm carries him away in the night.

decisions.choice: terrors: sudden, deadly dread
decisions.reason: Ballahot are the terrors that come with death and disaster; Bildad called death "the king of terrors" (18:11, 14).

decisions.choice: like waters: like a flood
decisions.reason: Floodwaters stand for overwhelming disaster (22:11; Psalm 69:2).

decisions.choice: a storm, a whirlwind
decisions.reason: Sufah is a violent storm wind; the wicked are "like chaff that the storm carries away" (21:18).

decisions.choice: a flood
decisions.reason: English "like waters" does not suggest danger; "a flood" does (m2).

source.text: יִשָּׂאֵ֣הוּ קָדִ֣ים וְיֵלַ֑ךְ וִֽ֝ישָׂעֲרֵ֗הוּ מִמְּקֹמֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Lifts him up [the] east wind and he goes, and it sweeps him away from his place.

en.L: The east wind lifts him up, and he is gone; \q it sweeps him away from his place.
en.B: The east wind picks him up, and he is gone; \q it sweeps him away from his place.
en.R: The hot desert wind picks him up, and he is gone. \q It blows him away from his home.

decisions.choice: the east wind: the scorching wind from the desert
decisions.reason: In the lands of the Bible the east wind blows hot and dry from the desert; it withers and destroys (Genesis 41:6; Hosea 13:15; Job 15:2; 38:24).

decisions.choice: from his place: gone from his home for good
decisions.reason: Job used the same words of the dead: "his place will not know him any more" (7:10; see 8:18; 20:9).

decisions.choice: the hot desert wind
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of wind the east wind is (m1).

source.text: וְיַשְׁלֵ֣ךְ עָ֭לָיו וְלֹ֣א יַחְמֹ֑ל מִ֝יָּד֗וֹ בָּר֥וֹחַ יִבְרָֽח׃

records.literal_gloss: And it throws at him and not it spares; from its hand fleeing he flees.

en.L: It hurls [itself] at him and does not spare; \q he flees headlong from its hand.
en.B: It hurls itself at him without mercy, \q as he flees headlong from its power.
en.R: It strikes him without mercy \q while he tries hard to escape its power.

decisions.choice: the subject is the wind of 27:21
decisions.reason: The verbs have no named subject. The east wind is the last one named, and it goes on in 27:23. Some read God as the one who throws, as in 6:4 and 16:13 where God's arrows strike Job; either way the storm is God's judgment.

decisions.choice: fleeing he flees: he runs for his life
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for force: he flees with all his might, and in vain.

decisions.choice: from its hand: from its power
decisions.reason: The hand stands for power (27:11).

decisions.choice: hurls itself
decisions.reason: The Hebrew verb has no object; Literal brackets "itself" and Balanced supplies it to make English sense.

source.text: יִשְׂפֹּ֣ק עָלֵ֣ימוֹ כַפֵּ֑ימוֹ וְיִשְׁרֹ֥ק עָ֝לָ֗יו מִמְּקֹמֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Claps at him his hands, and hisses at him from his place.

en.L: It claps its hands at him \q and hisses at him from his place.
en.B: It claps its hands at him \q and hisses at him from his place.
en.R: It claps and hisses at him in scorn \q as he is driven from his home.

decisions.choice: clapping and hissing: scorn at someone's ruin
decisions.reason: People clapped their hands and hissed over a fallen city or person to show contempt (Lamentations 2:15; Jeremiah 19:8; Zephaniah 2:15; Nahum 3:19).

decisions.choice: the wind, pictured as a person, mocks him
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject. The wind of 27:21-22 is the most likely, pictured as a person. It may also be impersonal, "people clap", the scorn of those who see his fall.

decisions.choice: his place: the man's home
decisions.reason: "His place" most likely means the home he is swept from, as in 27:21.

decisions.choice: in scorn / as he is driven
alternatives: claps its hands at him and hisses
decisions.reason: Readable says what the gestures mean (m1) and that he is being driven out (27:21).
